email.subject: Your parcel is on its way

body.v: Your parcel has left our depot and will be delivered tomorrow. You don't need to do anything.
You can also follow the delivery in the ParcelPoint app.

hotspots.explain: The address ends in parcelpoint.example: the carrier's real domain.
No deadline, no payment: it just tells you where your parcel is.
The link goes to parcelpoint.example, the real domain. Even so, the app is still the safest route.
It points you to the app, a channel you already have in hand.

who.prompt: Who is really writing to you? Read the address, not just the name.
who.answer: ParcelPoint: the address is on parcelpoint.example and the text is clean.
choices: A scammer with a near-identical address
A stranger using a free mailbox

emotion.prompt: Which feeling is this email pressing on?
emotion.answer: None. The message informs you, with no deadline and no pressure.
choices: None: it just keeps you informed
The lure of a free gift

ask.prompt: What does it actually want you to do?
ask.answer: Nothing. It tells you about the delivery and offers a tracking link.

verify.prompt: How can you check through a channel you control?
verify.answer: Nothing urgent to check. If you want to follow the delivery, open the ParcelPoint app yourself.
choices: Forward it to a relative for advice

actions.label: Open the ParcelPoint app yourself to check
actions.consequence: The same delivery date shows up. There was nothing to do.

actions.label: Do nothing and wait for the parcel
actions.consequence: The parcel arrives tomorrow, as announced.

actions.label: Reply with your home address, just in case
actions.consequence: Nobody reads replies sent to this notification address. No harm done, but no use either.

attacker_reveal: Not one of mine. It comes from ParcelPoint's domain, asks for nothing and sets no deadline. A real parcel notice keeps you posted; it doesn't get you to do anything.
